scenes.title: SQL Statements
scenes.narration: A SQL statement is a single complete instruction to the database, and they fall into a few clear families.

scenes.title: Families of statements
bullets: DDL defines structure, like CREATE and ALTER
DML changes data, like INSERT and UPDATE
scenes.narration: DDL statements such as CREATE and ALTER define the structure of your tables. DML statements like INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE change the data those tables hold. DQL, centered on SELECT, is how you read and query the data back out.

scenes.heading: DDL vs DML
scenes.narration: DDL statements shape the schema itself, creating or altering tables and other objects. DML statements instead work on the rows inside those tables, adding, changing, or removing data. Keeping the two straight helps you reason about what each command actually affects.

scenes.title: One statement, one job
scenes.narration: This single DML statement inserts one new row into the products table. The column list names which fields we are setting, and VALUES supplies the matching data. Because it ends with a semicolon, the database treats it as one complete instruction.

scenes.text: Grouping statements into DDL, DML, and DQL gives you a simple mental map of everything SQL can do.
scenes.narration: Thinking of statements as DDL, DML, and DQL families gives you a clear map of how each command fits into your work.
